title: Violence and abandonment

blocks.heading: Violence and abandonment
blocks.text: Gender-based violence concerns harmful acts linked to gender and unequal power; baby dumping is a distinct child-protection issue. Discuss interacting social risks and barriers to support without treating poverty or household type as proof of violence or abandonment. Responsibility for violence rests with the perpetrator, not the survivor.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
blocks.repair_note: Codex repair of Claude R6136 findings; preserved pre-repair baseline and action log in review/repairs/.

blocks.heading: GBV-related factors
blocks.text:
Unequal power, norms tolerating abuse, coercion and barriers to effective support can contribute to gender-based violence. Risk factors are not excuses or a prediction about an individual. An educational discussion should not request learners’ personal experiences or expose someone’s identity.

Applied example: A person claiming control over another’s choices may use threats or force, especially where norms excuse that behaviour. Unequal power can enable abuse, but responsibility remains with the person committing it.

blocks.heading: Baby dumping factors
blocks.text: Crisis, fear, stigma, coercion, isolation and difficulty reaching trusted support can interact around unsafe baby dumping. No single factor explains a particular case, and young or poor parents should not be labelled as likely offenders. Focus on protection and accessible qualified support, without providing unsafe instructions.

blocks.heading: A practical access test
blocks.text: A fictional information service receives few enquiries because callers expect their names to become public. Clear confidentiality arrangements, trained staff and a safe way to make first contact can reduce this barrier. Low use does not establish low need. Information about violence or child safety should focus on non-blaming support and competent services rather than require learners to disclose personal experiences.

blocks.heading: Protection is a coordinated task
blocks.text: Namibia’s 2012–2016 GBV plan, documented by [UNDP](https://www.undp.org/namibia/publications/namibia-national-plan-gender-based-violence-gbv-2012-2016), combined prevention, service implementation and survivor support, including a distinct infant-abandonment concern. This is a dated example. [UNICEF Namibia](https://www.unicef.org/namibia/child-protection) describes child protection through supportive family, community and institutional environments. Checked 20 October 2026; no current hotline or legal procedure is asserted.

blocks.heading: Recognise the issue and its different effects
blocks.text: Baby dumping means abandoning an infant, commonly a newborn, without appropriate care, exposing the child to danger and potentially death. It is distinct from seeking qualified support to keep a child safe. Contributing circumstances can include an unintended pregnancy, fear of losing education, lack of financial or partner support, coercion or violence, poor access to confidential information, and emotional crisis. They explain possible support needs, not an excuse or a prediction about a particular parent. Effects can include injury or death, lasting emotional harm to a surviving child, distress for family members, disruption of registration and care, and extra demands on protection services. Avoid using national death-rate changes as a substitute for explaining effects on the people involved.
context_tags: Codex repair after independent review; original teaching synthesis

blocks.heading: Types and contributing factors of gender-based violence
blocks.text: Gender-based violence includes physical and sexual violence; emotional abuse and economic control can also undermine safety and autonomy. Unequal power, entitlement and norms that excuse abuse can enable it. Substance misuse, exposure to violent behaviour and financial dependence can worsen risks or obstruct help, but neither poverty nor alcohol makes violence inevitable. Blaming clothing or the survivor shifts responsibility away from the person committing violence. Physical injury, distress, missed learning or work and the costs of obtaining protection can affect development. Name the type or mechanism required by a question rather than listing vague social problems.
